outputs.L1: Using the recently reported mode-locking effect, we demonstrate highly robust control of electron spin coherence in an ensemble of (In,Ga)As quantum dots over the single-spin coherence time. Spin precession in a transverse magnetic field can be fully controlled at temperatures up to 25 K by adjusting parameters of the pulsed-laser excitation protocol, such as the pulse-train sequence, thereby producing tunable quantum-beat bursts in Faraday rotation. We further demonstrate reversal of the electron spin-precession phase by inverting the polarization within a pulse-doublet sequence.
outputs.L2: Building on the newly observed mode-locking phenomenon, we achieve reliable manipulation of electron-spin coherence in an ensemble of (In,Ga)As quantum dots over the single-spin coherence timescale. In a transverse magnetic field, the precession dynamics can be precisely tuned at temperatures as high as 25 K by modifying parameters of the pulsed-laser excitation scheme, including the pulse-train arrangement, thereby producing controllable bursts of quantum beats in Faraday rotation. We also show that the phase of electron-spin precession can be reversed by switching the polarization within a double-pulse sequence.
outputs.L3:
The recently reported mode-locking effect enables highly robust control of electron-spin coherence in an ensemble of (In,Ga)As quantum dots. This control persists throughout the single-spin coherence time, allowing the coherent spin dynamics to be manipulated over the full relevant timescale. In a transverse magnetic field, electron-spin precession can be fully controlled at temperatures of up to 25 K.

The spin dynamics can also be tailored by modifying the pulsed-laser excitation protocol. In particular, adjusting the pulse-train sequence produces tunable bursts of quantum beats in the Faraday-rotation signal. Furthermore, within a pulse-doublet sequence, the phase of the electron-spin precession can be reversed simply by inverting the polarization of the optical excitation. Together, these capabilities demonstrate flexible and robust optical control of coherent electron-spin motion in quantum-dot ensembles.
outputs.L4:
Mode locking provides a powerful means of controlling electron-spin coherence in ensembles of self-assembled (In,Ga)As quantum dots. In a transverse magnetic field, optically generated electron spins precess at frequencies determined by their individual Larmor frequencies. Although variations in quantum-dot size, composition, and local environment normally cause rapid ensemble dephasing, a periodic train of circularly polarized laser pulses selectively reinforces those spin states whose precession periods are synchronized with the pulse repetition rate. The resulting phase synchronization produces a long-lived collective spin response that can be detected through time-resolved Faraday rotation.

By tailoring the timing and polarization of the excitation pulses, the synchronized spin ensemble can be manipulated with high precision. Pulse doublets introduce an additional controllable time interval, allowing specific precession modes to be enhanced or suppressed and thereby changing the frequency and phase of the observed Faraday-rotation quantum beats. Reversing the circular polarization of one pulse within a doublet reverses the optically induced spin orientation and can produce a corresponding phase reversal of the coherent precession signal.

This approach enabled full control of electron-spin precession at temperatures of up to 25 K. The persistence of mode locking under these conditions demonstrates the robustness of the synchronized spin coherence against thermal broadening and ensemble inhomogeneity. Adjustable quantum-beat patterns and polarization-controlled phase inversion show that pulse-sequence engineering can provide flexible all-optical control of collective spin dynamics in semiconductor quantum dots, with potential relevance to spin-based quantum information processing and coherent optoelectronic devices.
outputs.L5:
## Using the Faraday Cage

The Faraday cage, named after scientist Michael Faraday, is used to block electromagnetic fields. It is typically made from a continuous layer or mesh of conductive material. When an external electrical charge reaches the cage, the charge spreads across its outer surface, protecting the interior.

Today, Faraday cages are used in many practical applications. Microwave ovens contain metal shielding that keeps radiation inside, while laboratories use shielded rooms to prevent electromagnetic interference. Smaller Faraday pouches can also protect electronic devices and contactless cards from unwanted signals.

Using the Faraday cage demonstrates how a scientific discovery from the nineteenth century remains valuable in modern technology.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a concise abstract about robust optical control of electron spin coherence in an ensemble of (In,Ga)As quantum dots using mode locking and pulsed laser sequences.
counterfactuals.output: We demonstrate robust optical control of electron-spin coherence in an ensemble of self-assembled (In,Ga)As quantum dots. Periodic resonant excitation synchronizes spin precession through spin mode locking, overcoming ensemble inhomogeneity and extending coherent spin dynamics beyond the single-particle dephasing time. Tailored pulsed-laser sequences enable controlled spin rotations, refocusing, and selective manipulation of synchronized spin modes. The resulting coherence is resilient to variations in optical transition energies, precession frequencies, and pulse parameters. These findings establish mode-locked quantum-dot ensembles as a robust platform for ultrafast optical spin control and scalable semiconductor quantum technologies.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize a study demonstrating control of electron spin precession in a transverse magnetic field through pulse-train timing and polarization inversion.
counterfactuals.output: The study used a periodic train of circularly polarized laser pulses to initialize electron spins and monitored their Larmor precession in a transverse magnetic field with time-resolved Faraday/Kerr rotation. By adjusting the pulse spacing so that successive pulses arrived at selected phases of the precession, the researchers made the spin contributions interfere constructively or destructively, selecting and phase-locking particular precession modes. Reversing the pulse helicity inverted the injected spin direction, shifting the synchronization condition by half a Larmor cycle. Thus, without changing the magnetic field, pulse timing and polarization inversion provided optical control over the amplitude and phase of the collective electron-spin precession.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a research-paper abstract describing adjustable quantum beat bursts in Faraday rotation, electron spin coherence control up to 25 K, and phase flipping with a pulse doublet sequence.
counterfactuals.output: We demonstrate tunable bursts of quantum beats in time-resolved Faraday rotation arising from coherent electron-spin precession. Using a pulse-doublet sequence, we further induce a controlled phase flip of the spin precession through interference between independently generated coherences. counterfactuals.prompt: How can the recently reported mode-locking effect be used to manipulate electron spin coherence and precession phase in (In,Ga)As quantum dots?
counterfactuals.output:
Mode locking turns a periodically pumped, inhomogeneous ensemble of electron spins into a set of synchronized precession modes.

- A train of circularly polarized laser pulses initializes the resident electron spins through the trion transition.
- Only dots whose Larmor frequency satisfies  
  \[
  \omega_L T_R = 2\pi N
  \]
  with pulse repetition period \(T_R\), return to the same orientation when the next pulse arrives. Repeated excitation reinforces these spins while other phases largely cancel.
- The result is a long-lived spin signal that revives just before each pulse, even when the ensemble dephasing time \(T_2^*\) is short. Its decay reflects the much longer homogeneous coherence time \(T_2\).

This provides two control knobs:

1. **Coherence control:** Changing the pulse repetition rate, magnetic field, or number of preparation pulses selects different synchronized Larmor-frequency modes and controls how strongly the ensemble is phase focused. Hyperfine-driven nuclear feedback can further stabilize these modes.

2. **Precession-phase control:** The timing, helicity, area, and detuning of an additional optical pulse can reset or rotate the synchronized spins. Shifting the pulse arrival time changes the reference phase; a suitably chosen control pulse can impose a phase jump, reverse the observed oscillation, or prepare a desired phase relative to subsequent pulses.

Thus, mode locking allows optical pulse sequences to convert a rapidly dephasing quantum-dot ensemble into a coherent spin packet and to program both its lifetime and its Larmor-precession phase.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a brief scientific summary of an experiment in which pulsed optical excitation controls spin precession during the single-spin coherence time, including the effects of pulse sequence and polarization.
counterfactuals.output: An experiment used time-resolved pump–probe spectroscopy to control the Larmor precession of individual spins within their coherence time. A first optical pulse initialized a coherent spin state, while subsequent pulses, applied before dephasing, modified its phase and amplitude. The response depended strongly on pulse timing: sequences synchronized with the precession reinforced coherence, whereas phase-shifted or nonsynchronous pulses suppressed or reversed the oscillation. Circularly polarized pulses produced spin-selective rotations whose direction changed with helicity, while linearly polarized pulses caused little net spin orientation and primarily served as a reference. These results demonstrate coherent, polarization-dependent optical control of spin dynamics on timescales shorter than the single-spin coherence time.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
